name: Blind Don
description: Blind Don is the strategic two-player variation of Nine-Card Don, a traditional British pub game from the All Fours family. Popular in Lancashire and South Wales, it features a unique two-part deal where players play through the entire deck in two separate phases. The game centers on capturing high-point cards, particularly the Nines and the 'Don' (Five of Trumps). It is a game of perfect memory, as the cards played in the first half reveal the exact contents of the opponent's hand in the second half.

history.origins: Descended from the 17th-century game All Fours via the Irish game Dom Pedro. 'Don' emerged as a distinct British regional variant, with Blind Don being the adaptation for two players to maintain the competitive tension of the partnership version.
timeline: 1800s: All Fours variants like Dom Pedro spread through the UK and Ireland.
1900s: Nine-Card Don becomes a staple pub game in Lancashire.
Present: Survival as a niche traditional game in British regional card clubs.
history.cultural: Reflects the 'Old School' British pub gaming culture where memory and card-counting are highly respected skills.
history.evolution: The game's 'two-part' deal structure was developed to allow two players to use the full deck while maintaining small, manageable hand sizes.

setup.deck: Standard 52-card French pack. Ranks: A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2.
setup.dealing: Deal 13 cards to each player. The remaining 26 cards are set aside face-down for the second half of the game. The first card played (the 'pitch') by the non-dealer sets the trump suit for the entire hand.

rules.objective: Score points by capturing specific cards in tricks. Points: Nines (9 each), Fives (5 each), Aces (4 each), Kings (3), Queens (2), Jacks (1).
rules.gameplay: 1. **Part One**: Play 13 tricks with the first deal. Trump is set by the first card led. 2. **Part Two**: Deal the remaining 26 cards (13 each). Play the remaining 13 tricks using the same trump suit. 3. **The Play**: Must follow suit if possible. If void, may trump or discard.
keyRules: The Five of Trumps is known as the 'Don'.
Winning the last trick of the game (the 26th trick) scores no bonus points, but captures the cards.
Players must follow suit if they can; trumps rank high.

strategy.basic: Prioritize capturing the Nines. Since a single Nine is worth 9 points (more than an Ace and King combined), it is the most efficient way to build a lead.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Part Two' Advantage: Use the first 13 tricks to identify which high cards your opponent is holding. In the second half, you will know exactly which suits they are void in.
strategy.advanced: Trump Control: Save your 'Don' (5 of trumps) to capture an opponent's high-point Nine when they are forced to lead it or play it on a side-suit void.
tips: Never lead a Nine unless you are certain it will win the trick.
Count the trumps carefully; there are 13 in total across both phases.

scoring.description: Points are tallied after all 26 tricks. First to reach 80 points wins the match.

synthesis.shortDescription: A strategic two-player variation of Nine-Card Don from Northern England. Pitch a card to set the trump, battle through 13 tricks, then deal the rest and play with perfect knowledge. With Nines worth a massive 9 points each, every play is a high-stakes calculation.
